newsitem.title: USA: AMR pilots see strike costing up to $40 mln/day.
newsitem.headline: AMR pilots see strike costing up to $40 mln/day.

text.p: Pilots of American Airlines expect a strike would cost the company $9-$40 million a day with a total impact of a strike reaching up to $1.4 billion.
The strike would cost about $25 million a day on weekends and $40 million a day on weekdays.
If American forced a "lockout", or shut down the airline, it would cost $9 million a day for the duration of the strike.
The pilot's union estimates the 30-day "cooling off period" will cost the company $177 million due to lost bookings as customers shy away from American Airlines.
American declined to comment on the pilot's cost estimates. But the airline said earlier that a 60-day strike would hurt the U.S. economy by $4.75 billion.
American and its pilots entered the cooling off period after the pilots rejected a wage proposal last month.
The union will meet with AMR Corp's management on Thursday to present the pilot's proposal and its economic impact on the company.
The Allied Pilot's Association briefed analysts and institutional investors Tuesday about their proposal to the airline's management.
The pilot's union said their demands would cost the airline $285 million more over the course of the contract as compared with the contract that was previously rejected.
"If you look at the profits that American is supposed to see, you would not think $62 million a year would be insurmountable," said James Sovich, President of the pilot's union.

Sovich did not believe the relationship between the union and management had improved during the 30-day cooling off period. The pilot's union said it wants to reach a settlement, but it is willing to strike.
The pilots can strike February 15 if last ditch negotiations next week fail. The last round of formal talks between the union and management will begin February 10.
"We do not want to strike, but we are willing to strike. We've made a very balanced offer," Sovich said.
The pilots said their proposal offers the company $212 million over five years in productivity concessions.

Sovich said that, although the strike would have short term negative effects on the company and the airline industry, he dismissed speculation by analysts that AMR management would cut operations and sell the airline if it was forced to meet the pilot's demands.
"If $285 million is the difference between modest growth at the airline or selling the airline that's very short- sighted," Sovich said.
The pilots are seeking pay raises, stock options and the elimination of a two-tier pay scale. The pilots also oppose having regional jets flown by pilots of a different union.
